intro: Three kinds of dance share the same triple metre: a heavy-footed Ländler, a faster waltz and a slower, gentler Ländler. Mahler brings them back in altered combinations, until the original dance ends in scattered instrumental fragments.
question: How can the same three-beat metre produce such different kinds of movement?

cues.title: A deliberately clumsy dance
cues.text: Mahler asks for the tempo of a leisurely Ländler, “somewhat clumsy and very coarse”. Bassoons and violas supply a short upbeat figure; clarinets answer before the string dance gathers momentum.
cues.evidence: The score heading and opening orchestration are described in Lew Smoley’s guide. The report starts quietly and has a marked level increase and boundary around 0:20; the description covers successive opening gestures.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three beats, unequal weight
cues.text: Try counting three beats through the dance without giving each equal emphasis. Mahler’s accents and short upbeats make the gait deliberately awkward; triple metre alone does not make a smooth waltz.
cues.evidence: The written metre and opening articulation establish the listening exercise. The report’s automatic tempo is not used as a count of the performed beat.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Fiddles rather than polish
cues.text: The string instruction “Wie Fiedeln” asks for a fiddle-like character. Listen for the difference between the tune’s simple shape and the deliberately ungainly way it is articulated.
cues.evidence: Smoley documents “Wie Fiedeln” in the opening Ländler; the report remains in the opening C-major region through 2:50. The cue applies to the paragraph, not an instruction newly reached at 1:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A summer’s draft
cues.text: Mahler completed the Ninth’s draft at Toblach on 2 September 1909. The work catalogue distinguishes that summer draft from the fair-copy full score, prepared in New York during the following winter and spring.
cues.evidence: Mahler-Online, GMW 50, composition history: https://acdh-ch.pages.oeaw.ac.at/muwi/mahler-mei/mahler-wv-static/GMW_050.html
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A dance clears the floor
cues.text: The original Ländler dwindles before the faster dance takes over. Notice that the change in pace need not change the number of beats in the bar.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −28.1 dB at 2:40 to −36.9 at 2:50, then rises sharply at 2:55 with greater onset density. The score identifies the succeeding Tempo II waltz.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The waltz changes the gait
cues.text: Tempo II is a quicker waltz, initially centred on E major. The new dance keeps triple metre but abandons the first Ländler’s deliberate tread; its turns become increasingly forceful.
cues.evidence: The score and Smoley establish Tempo II and E major. The local report changes sharply at 2:55 and shows E-major-compatible pitch content around 3:10–3:35; this confirms only the broad region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight inside the whirl
cues.text: The waltz does not remain light. This stretch reaches a conspicuous early crest, showing how quickly a dance rhythm can acquire orchestral force.
cues.evidence: The report lists 4:00 among the highest five-second windows; further high-level windows occur at 4:25–4:30. No particular brass attack is inferred from those measurements.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A slower dance approaches
cues.text: As the waltz loses momentum, listen for a gentler treatment of the same three-beat framework. The third dance is another Ländler, not a change into duple metre.
cues.evidence: The score’s Tempo III slow Ländler follows the first waltz. A boundary at 4:56 and the drop across 4:50–5:00 anchor the approaching change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Falling steps, longer breath
cues.text: The slower Ländler brings a more spacious falling-step melody. Its F-major setting and lighter movement contrast with the preceding waltz, though brief returns of other dance figures interrupt its continuity.
cues.evidence: Smoley identifies the F-major slow Ländler and interleaved Tempo I recollection. The report shows reduced onset density and quieter F-major-compatible regions around 4:50–5:25 and 6:00–6:20; it does not establish each individual switch.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Small steps can travel
cues.text: The falling two-note shape also matters in the first movement. Hear how a small melodic interval can connect unlike characters without making the dances quotations of an entire earlier tune.
cues.evidence: Smoley relates the slow Ländler’s falling-second material to the first movement. This is a motivic comparison across movements, not an asserted exact quotation at 6:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The waltz regains momentum
cues.text: The quicker dance returns in a changed tonal setting, now around D major. A return in this movement means recognisable rhythm and contour, not an exact replay in the original key.
cues.evidence: The written Tempo II return is in D major. The strong 6:30 boundary and increased onset density with D-major-compatible content at 6:40–7:00 anchor this region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A festival of ninths
cues.text: The 1912 festival that introduced Mahler’s Ninth also programmed Beethoven’s Ninth under Felix Weingartner and Bruckner’s Ninth under Arthur Nikisch. Walter’s premiere placed the new work beside two established symphonic predecessors.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, p. 1, identifies the three Ninths and their conductors: https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Follow the changing accents
cues.text: The dances are distinguished by their accents and phrase lengths as much as by tempo. Try keeping the bar’s three beats in mind while the upper parts lean across them or stretch a phrase beyond its expected ending.
cues.evidence: General score-based listening exercise for the alternating dances; no precise accent or metrical displacement is assigned to this second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A sequence of withdrawals
cues.text: The busy middle stretch repeatedly loses weight, with short renewed gestures between the reductions. Listen for the way a return can emerge from the remnants of another dance rather than after a clean stop.
cues.evidence: The report marks boundaries at 8:46, 8:56, 9:02, 9:16 and 9:22, culminating in a very low window at 9:25. This cue describes the measured fragmentation, not a named cadence.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The first dance in miniature
cues.text: The original Ländler returns through a much more exposed texture. Solo viola, cello and violin writing makes the familiar figures less collective than they sounded at the beginning.
cues.evidence: The score-derived late Tempo I return is described by Smoley. The report has its quietest internal window at 9:25 and stays comparatively low through 9:50 before the sound gains weight.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognise the upbeat
cues.text: Instead of following only the longest tune, listen for the little rising upbeat from the opening. A short figure can identify a dance even when its melody is shared between different instruments.
cues.evidence: The opening four-sixteenth upbeat recurs in the score. This is an invitation to compare its versions, not a claim that a specific instrument begins it at 10:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The quieter return is challenged
cues.text: The texture gathers weight again and the faster dance interrupts. The contrast is no longer simply between successive dances: their gestures press against one another within the larger span.
cues.evidence: The score places another aggressive Tempo II episode after the reduced Tempo I return. Relative level rises at 10:40, with higher onset density at 11:00 and the movement’s highest windows at 11:05–11:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Momentum without a new metre
cues.text: Listen for the tension between increased momentum and the underlying three-beat organisation. Mahler can make the dance feel increasingly difficult to contain without discarding its basic metre.
cues.evidence: The score’s later waltz retains triple metre while increasing intensity and speed. The cue does not use onset counts as a metronome reading.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Five rehearsals for the microphones
cues.text: Gaisberg arranged for an engineer to test microphone placement during five rehearsals before the 1938 concert. This live recording was planned in advance, not an accidental document discovered afterwards.
cues.evidence: Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 2, quotes Gaisberg’s account of five rehearsals and microphone tests.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A final forceful exchange
cues.text: The later dance conflict gathers another strong crest before the first Ländler takes over for the close. Listen for the abrupt difference in scale when the accumulated sound is withdrawn.
cues.evidence: The report rises from the lower 12:25–12:35 windows towards 13:00, then shows strong boundaries at 13:04, 13:16 and 13:20 and a sharp level drop at 13:20.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The Ländler comes apart
cues.text: The last return restores the original dance, but its phrases increasingly break into separate instrumental gestures. This is a return of material, not a restoration of the opening’s uninterrupted ensemble texture.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the concluding Tempo I and gradual fragmentation. The 13:20 boundary anchors its broad onset, while the score’s final pages show isolated woodwind and string fragments.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A figure changes its owner
cues.text: In the closing pages, listen for familiar scraps passing between winds and strings. Their identity survives the change of register and timbre; the increasingly separated replies make the dance easier to hear in pieces.
cues.evidence: Score, final pages of movement II, especially printed p. 103, shows solo wind and string fragments. The report’s lower-level 14:00–14:30 region anchors this late texture broadly.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Walter’s account is an interpretation
cues.text: In his 1936 book on Mahler, Walter described this movement as a world where “the dance is over”. His words record the conductor’s response; they are not a programme supplied by Mahler.
cues.evidence: Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 3, quotes Walter’s 1936 account of the second movement. Attribution is retained rather than converted into the composer’s intention.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The ends of the orchestra
cues.text: At the close, piccolo and contrabassoon bring the high and low extremes together with short rising figures. Plucked upper strings supply the final small punctuation, far removed from the earlier waltz crests.
cues.evidence: First-edition score, printed p. 103, final bars: piccolo, contrabassoon and pizzicato upper strings. The report descends across 15:20–15:40 towards the 15:46 file end; this is a closing-passage cue, not the exact last attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A quicker dance changes the accent pattern
transitions.how: The C-major Ländler diminishes before Tempo II introduces the faster E-major waltz. The metre stays in three, but the strings’ more flowing movement replaces the earlier blunt upbeat and heavy tread. Shared short figures connect the dances even as the new tempo and tonal region make the contrast unmistakable.
transitions.evidence: Written Tempo II and E-major setting; this report’s level jump between 2:50 and 2:55 and increased attack density anchor the approximate change.

transitions.title: The faster dance releases a slower melody
transitions.how: The first waltz loses weight and speed before the F-major Tempo III Ländler. Its falling-step melody and more spacious phrases replace the waltz’s forward pressure. Short reminders of the original dance interrupt this slower region, so the passage is not a self-contained trio followed by a mechanical repeat.
transitions.evidence: The score and Smoley establish the F-major Tempo III and interjections. The report’s 4:56 boundary, level decrease and lower onset density around 5:00 locate the broad change.

transitions.title: The waltz resumes in a new key
transitions.how: The slower dance’s space contracts as Tempo II returns, now around D major. Active strings and the renewed dance pulse carry the change of pace; the waltz is recognisable despite its altered key and continuation. Mahler transforms a previous section rather than inserting an unchanged repeat.
transitions.evidence: Score-defined return; a strong boundary at 6:30 precedes increased onset density and D-major-compatible pitch content around 6:40–7:00.

transitions.title: A dwindling texture restores the original dance
transitions.how: The mixed dance activity slows and thins. The original Ländler returns in exposed viola, cello and violin lines rather than its opening ensemble dress. Its C-major orientation and familiar upbeat provide continuity, while the reduced scoring makes the return tentative and fragmented.
transitions.evidence: The score-derived Tempo I return follows the interrupted middle span. Boundaries at 9:16 and 9:22 lead to the quiet 9:25 window and gradual recovery after 9:30.

transitions.title: Faster material interrupts the restored Ländler
transitions.how: The quieter first dance gains weight before another Tempo II interruption. Strings and brass enlarge the faster dance figures, and the phrase pushes beyond the steadier Ländler gait. The connection rests on recurring upbeats and falling figures, but their stronger articulation makes the change feel confrontational.
transitions.evidence: The score and Smoley describe the later waltz invasion. The report rises at 10:40 and reaches its largest windows at 11:05–11:10; the marker is an approximate approach.

transitions.title: The first dance returns and loses continuity
transitions.how: The last forceful exchange yields to Tempo I and the original C-major dance. Rather than rebuilding its opening texture, Mahler lets separate wind and string lines retain only pieces of the material. The long closing reduction ends with piccolo and contrabassoon figures and a small pizzicato punctuation.
transitions.evidence: The report’s strong 13:20 boundary and level fall locate the final return region. The closing scoring is visible on printed p. 103 of the full score.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement II, especially the opening and printed p. 103. Passage-level scoring highlights; intermediate formal placement follows Smoley and local feature anchors, not bar alignment.

timeline.note: Opening exchanges: bassoons and violas supply the upbeat, with clarinets answering; these are successive gestures.
Opening Ländler: the second violins carry the rough-edged dance tune within the growing texture.
Tempo II region: active string writing changes the gait into a faster waltz.
Slow Ländler region: horn and strings shape the gentler falling-step material.
Reduced Tempo I return: the original dance emerges through exposed string lines.
Later waltz region: brass and active strings enlarge the faster dance’s weight.
Closing pages: small wind and string fragments replace the preceding collective texture.
Final-bars preview: piccolo and contrabassoon rise at opposite extremes; upper strings finish pizzicato.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
